cells.tense: You are tending a thing that is finishing, and you know it is finishing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've brought to the point where it works on its own, and hand it off this week, even if the handoff is imperfect.
cells.core:
You've been at this a while. What you're growing has started to hold its own shape, and you can feel when it turns the corner — when less of your hand is needed, not more. You notice the difference between the support it still wants and the support it no longer does. That noticing is the work now.

The release doesn't have to be dramatic. It can be as small as walking away from a thing for a day and letting it run, or saying yes to someone else taking the next step. What you're carrying is finishing. The part that's yours now is setting it down clean.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what's finished and let it stand without you.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing until it can hold itself
cells.place: At a point of completion that has to be let out the door

cells.tense: You will keep the help going long after the thing has learned to stand without it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're still holding open, and let a whole day pass without checking on it — no message, no adjustment, no look.
cells.core:
This works best as patient watching: you set the conditions, then you see what the growing thing shows you it needed, and you stay curious instead of supervising. You can water something and then leave it alone for a day. You can tell the part that was yours from the part that is the thing's own life.

What's ahead in your head is the day it finally works, where you finally get it right, and you already live there. So you check, you adjust, you hold the door open a little longer, and holding it has started to replace the thing it was for. Push harder and the loop never closes. Step back far enough and it finishes in its own shape, not the one you keep rehearsing.
cells.sheetLine: You keep tending past the point where it needed you.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing until it can hold itself

cells.tense: You stopped tending before the thing was done, and you've been standing at that door since.
cells.ask: Choose one unfinished thing you walked away from, take one small concrete step back toward it today, and don't decide yet whether it's worth finishing.
cells.core:
Something got left half-grown. You know it — you can name it faster than you'd like to. Since then you've kept your hands on small things that don't risk much, projects that finish quickly and ask nothing of you in the middle. The growing sits unused, and the not-using it has started to look like not caring.

Care is not what went missing. What went missing is the willingness to stand inside something unfinished that isn't working yet. That middle is survivable. It only needs one small act of attention on a thing you actually want to see through, without needing to know yet how it ends.
cells.sheetLine: You left something half-grown and stopped showing up for the middle.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing until it can hold itself
cells.place: At a point of completion that has to be let out the door

cells.tense: You are already growing things here and you talk about it as if it were happening on its own.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person, that a thing you've been treating as a situation was actually something you grew, and name the act you did.
cells.core:
It runs cleanly when you set the conditions and then let what's growing show you what it needed — you water, then you wait. You can name the part that was yours and the part that was the thing's own life, and you let the second part happen without standing over it.

Right now you're tending more than you'd admit. The room gets shaped, the thing gets moved, the person gets fed — and you describe it as if the situation required it, or the day did it. The growing is real; the ownership isn't spoken. Name one of them out loud and you get the choice back: keep doing it, or stop.
